title: Hybrid Quantum Network for classification of finance and MNIST data
journal_or_venue: 2021 IEEE 18th International Conference on Software Architecture Companion (ICSA-C)
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a hybrid quantum-classical neural network that places a parametrized quantum circuit between classical encoder and decoder networks and uses TensorFlow Quantum for training. It demonstrates the approach on a credit-scoring finance dataset and on MNIST, reporting improved performance (ACC/AUC and faster convergence) compared with a similarly sized classical network while highlighting issues with overfitting and the need for regularization and hardware-noise studies.
methodology_description: The authors design and evaluate a hybrid classical–quantum neural network (QNet) for supervised classification on realistic datasets (finance credit-scoring and MNIST). The hybrid architecture places a classical encoding neural network in front of a parametrized quantum circuit and a classical post-processing network after the quantum measurements. The classical encoder maps input features to rotation angles (parameters) used in per-qubit encoding gates; encoding consists of R_y(phi1)·R_z(phi2)·R_y(phi3) on each qubit followed by CNOT entangling. A variational (parametrized) quantum ansatz U(φ) composed of per-qubit rotation layers (R_y, R_z, R_z combinations) and CNOT entangling layers is applied; the variational block is repeatable nlayers times. Two variants are compared: (a) encoding once then repeating only the variational block, and (b) data re-uploading where the encoding block is repeated between variational blocks (per Perez‑Salinas et al.). Measurements are post-processed by a classical output network; final classification uses softmax activation and categorical cross-entropy loss. Training is performed end-to-end (classical and quantum parameters) via gradient-based optimization using the Adam optimizer. Baseline comparisons use a purely classical neural net (NNet) with a single hidden layer sized to have a comparable number of parameters. Performance is evaluated on train/test splits using accuracy (ACC) and area under the ROC curve (AUC); confusion matrices are reported for MNIST. Experiments are executed in simulation with TensorFlow Quantum on a conventional notebook (16 GB RAM, Intel i7), and reported results compare QNet (with and without data re-uploading) to the matched classical baseline.
algorithms_used: Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC / Parametrized Quantum Circuit)
experimental_setup: Simulated quantum experiments using TensorFlow Quantum on a conventional notebook (Intel i7 CPU, 16 GB RAM). No physical QPU runs reported; Google quantum hardware access was restricted so all experiments used the TFQ simulator.
dataset_used: Finance: Lending Club credit scoring dataset (Kaggle: wordsforthewise/lending-club), reduced to samples with 6 features scaled to [0,1]; two training samples prepared: (I) balanced (default rate 50%) with 340 training observations, (II) unbalanced (original default ~16.67%) with 900 training observations. MNIST: MNIST image dataset (greyscale 28x28); experiments used 1,000 training images and the full 10,000-image test set in reported runs.

finance_dataset.preprocessing: Features scaled to [0,1]; two sample variants constructed: balanced sample I (default rate 50%, 340 training samples) and unbalanced sample II (original default ~16.67%, 900 training samples).

mnist_dataset.preprocessing: Classical encoder network used to downscale 784 inputs to the number of quantum circuit parameters (i.e., to match available qubits). Training subset: 1,000 images; test set: 10,000 images.

pipeline_steps: Preprocess inputs (scaling to [0,1] for finance; flatten images for MNIST).
Classical encoding neural network maps input features to parameter vectors (angles) for quantum encoding; design matches number of qubits.
Quantum encoding per qubit: R_y(phi1) -> R_z(phi2) -> R_y(phi3), where phi values come from encoder output.
Apply CNOT gates to entangle qubits after encoding.
Apply variational ansatz U(phi): on each qubit apply rotation sequence (R_y, R_z, R_z) plus CNOT entangling; repeat this variational block nlayers times.
Variant: data re-uploading repeats the encoding block between variational layers (encoding + variational repeated nlayers times).
Measure qubits; feed measurement results into a classical output neural network with softmax activation.

Train entire hybrid model end-to-end using categorical cross-entropy loss and Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.01); compare to classical NNet baseline with one hidden layer having approximately equal parameter count.
notable_parameters_and_choices: Reported experiments used n_qubits = n_layers = 8 (finance experiments).
Number of variational parameters n = 3 * n_qubits * n_layers (for the variational part).
Loss: categorical cross-entropy; optimizer: Adam with lr=0.01.
Metrics tracked: training and test ACC, AUC; confusion matrix for MNIST.

outputs_and_findings: QNet (with data re-uploading) yielded higher training ACC/AUC than classical NNet in reported settings; also exhibited faster training convergence on MNIST.

Data re-uploading variant generally outperformed the variant without re-uploading in reported experiments.

reproducibility_notes: Datasets are referenced (Kaggle lending‑club link and MNIST). The paper specifies the architecture, gate sequences, optimizer, learning rate and principal hyperparameters (n_qubits, n_layers). No code or explicit training hyperparameters (epochs, batch size, random seeds) are provided in the text and no code repository is cited, so full reproduction would require reimplementation of the described architecture and choices; dataset sourcing is possible from the referenced links.
key_findings: [supported] A hybrid architecture (classical encoder -> parametrized quantum circuit -> classical post-processor) can be implemented and trained in simulation (TensorFlow Quantum) to perform binary and multiclass classification on non-trivial datasets (finance credit scoring and MNIST).

[supported] Using a classical neural network to encode (downscale) high-dimensional classical data into a smaller set of parameters enables handling high-dimensional inputs (e.g., MNIST 784 features) with a limited number of qubits.

[supported] Data re-uploading (repeating the data-encoding circuit together with variational layers) improved empirical performance over repeating only the variational part in the reported experiments.

[supported] For the balanced finance sample (sample I) with nqubits=nlayers=8 the QNet with data re-uploading achieved ACCtrain=0.78, AUCtrain=0.86, ACCtest=0.68, AUCtest=0.72 (reported), which differed from classical NNet behaviour on the same task.

[supported] For the unbalanced finance sample (sample II) with nqubits=nlayers=8 the QNet (with re-uploading) obtained ACCtrain=0.84, AUCtrain=0.77, ACCtest=0.84, AUCtest=0.55 (reported), slightly outperforming the classical NNet on AUCtrain and AUCtest in that setting.

[supported] On a reduced MNIST experiment (1,000 training images, full 10,000 test images) the QNet converged faster during training and achieved ACCtrain=0.98 and ACCtest=0.81 (reported); the classical baseline had ACCtrain=0.83 and ACCtest=0.81.
[supported] Overfitting is observed for the hybrid QNet in multiple experiments (notably strong on MNIST), indicating need for regularization of the hybrid architecture.

[supported] TensorFlow Quantum (simulator) was practical for the experiments: the authors report being able to simulate relatively large circuits (e.g., 10 qubits × 10 layers) on a 16 GB notebook in a few hours.

[speculative] The paper suggests that, more generally, the hybrid QNet approach can outperform classical networks of similar parameter count across data types, but this is asserted beyond the limited empirical cases presented.
[speculative] Entanglement of qubits is expected to improve QML performance (statement of expectation rather than demonstrated in this paper).
[speculative] A consistent regularization scheme combining classical and quantum parts is desirable and necessary to control overfitting (proposal for future work).

[speculative] Results obtained in simulator can be translated to hardware and the approach can be deployed to mobile/web contexts using the TensorFlow ecosystem (projection; authors note limited hardware access).
results_summary: The paper implements a hybrid classical-quantum neural network (classical encoder → parametrized quantum circuit → classical decoder) using TensorFlow Quantum and evaluates it on two finance classification samples (balanced and unbalanced) and a reduced MNIST experiment. Empirically, the hybrid model (QNet) with data re-uploading often converged faster and showed improved training metrics versus a classical neural net with comparable parameter count; in several reported metrics (ACC/AUC) QNet outperformed the classical baseline on the tested instances, though overfitting was observed (particularly on MNIST). Data re-uploading improved performance compared to reusing only variational layers. The work is simulation-based and the authors highlight the need for regularization and further study, including evaluations on real quantum hardware.

quantum_advantage_detail: The authors report instances where the hybrid QNet outperforms a classical network of similar parameter count in simulation (faster training convergence and some higher ACC/AUC metrics on the tested datasets). However results are simulation-based, dataset- and hyperparameter-specific, mixed across metrics (e.g., some classical AUCtest values are higher), and the study is small-scale — so a definitive, general quantum advantage is not demonstrated and remains speculative.
limitations: NISQ-era hardware constraints: limited qubit counts and limited circuit depth restrict direct application of many VQC encoding schemes (author-stated).
Common VQC encoding scales the number of qubits with the number of classical features, making direct encoding of high-dimensional inputs infeasible on current hardware (author-stated).
Experiments were run on simulators due to restrictive access to quantum hardware; results therefore reflect idealized, noise-free conditions (author-stated).
Observed overfitting of the hybrid QNet on unseen data (finance and MNIST experiments), indicating the models can lack generalization (author-stated).
No consistent or developed regularization scheme for the quantum or hybrid network was implemented; regularization methods to prevent overfitting are lacking (author-stated).
Evaluation relied on limited metrics (accuracy and AUC) and the authors note accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced data — broader metric choices/interpretation are required (author-stated).

Access and deployment limitations: Google TensorFlow Quantum gives good simulation/development support but hardware access is restrictive, limiting transfer to production quantum devices (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Proposes and evaluates a hybrid classical–quantum neural network (classical encoder -> parametrized quantum circuit -> classical decoder) trained end-to-end on classification tasks.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Reports improved training ACC/AUC and faster convergence of the QNet (with data re-uploading) versus a parameter-matched classical neural net on small simulated finance and MNIST tasks.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments target NISQ-style variational circuits (8 qubits, 8 layers) and explicitly discuss overfitting and the need for hardware-noise studies, indicating cautious near-term applicability.
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments run in TensorFlow Quantum simulator; no runs on physical QPUs were performed.
#limitation:qubit-count — Uses only n_qubits = 8 (and reduces input dimensionality via classical encoder), raising concerns about applicability to full-scale financial feature sets.

#limitation:data-encoding — Uses a classical encoder to map inputs to rotation angles and downsamples MNIST to match qubit capacity, highlighting encoding/bottleneck issues for high-dimensional financial data.
#limitation:noise — Notes need for hardware-noise studies; results are reported for ideal (noiseless) simulation which may not reflect real-device performance.
contradictions: Paper reports a quantum advantage (higher training ACC/AUC and faster convergence) but the advantage is demonstrated only in simulator experiments on small datasets and is accompanied by pronounced overfitting (e.g., MNIST train ACC 0.98 vs test ACC 0.81), undermining claims of practical superiority over classical models (contradiction:classical-vs-quantum).

The study uses 8 qubits and a classical encoder that reduces input dimensionality; this limits conclusions about scaling to real-world financial problems and contradicts any implication that the approach is readily scalable to production-size datasets (contradiction:scalability).
